results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No. A permanent phasing in does not trigger enter-the-battlefield abilities (enters-the-battlefield triggers). Phasing is a special status change, not a zone change: during phasing a permanent’s status becomes phased out and it’s treated as though it doesn’t exist except where rules say otherwise, and when it phases in its status becomes phased in and the game treats it as though it exists again ([702.26a], [702.26b], [702.26c]). "Enter-the-battlefield" abilities are zone-change triggers that trigger when a permanent actually enters the battlefield ([603.6a]). Because the phasing event doesn’t actually cause a permanent to change zones or control, zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out ([702.26d]). (For completeness: abilities that trigger when a permanent phases out are handled specially and “look back in time” to determine whether they trigger ([603.10b]); that exception applies to phasing-out triggers, not to enters-the-battlefield triggers.)

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text:
Direct answer: When an attacking creature has both trample and deathtouch, you need only assign 1 point of combat damage to each blocking creature (unless damage is already marked or other creatures are assigning damage at the same time), and you may assign the rest of that attacking creature’s combat damage to the defending player/planeswalker/battle as permitted by trample.

Explanation and definitions
- Deathtouch: Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is treated as lethal damage for the purpose of determining excess damage [702.2c]. For game effects that destroy after deathtouch damage, a creature dealt damage by a source with deathtouch is destroyed as a state-based action (damage is first marked on the creature) [302.7, 702.2b, 704.5h].
- Trample: Trample modifies how an attacking creature assigns combat damage. The controller of an attacking creature with trample assigns damage to blocking creatures first; once each blocking creature has been assigned lethal damage, any excess may be assigned to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle as the controller chooses (subject to trample’s special rules for planeswalkers) [702.19a, 702.19b, 702.19c].
- Lethal damage and excess damage: Lethal damage is an amount greater than or equal to a creature’s toughness (taking into account damage already marked and other creatures assigning damage at the same time) [Lethal Damage, 120.4a]. When the source dealing damage has deathtouch, any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage (so 1 damage is treated as lethal for assignment purposes) [120.4a].

Putting those rules together: during the combat damage assignment step you treat 1 point of damage from the deathtouch trample source as enough to be “lethal” to each blocking creature (unless that creature already has damage marked or other creatures are assigning damage that also counts toward lethal), so you assign at least 1 to each blocker and may assign the remainder to the defending player/planeswalker/battle as allowed by the trample rules [702.19b, 120.4a, 702.2c]. After damage is dealt and marked, state-based actions will destroy any creature that was dealt deathtouch damage [302.7, 702.2b, 704.5h].

Timing assumption: this explanation assumes normal combat damage assignment and dealing in the combat damage step (assigning follows the rules in 510.1 and trample assignment rules). If damage is already marked on a blocker or other attackers are assigning damage at the same time, the amount you must assign to that blocker may be reduced accordingly because you must take marked and concurrently assigned damage into account when determining what is lethal [702.19b, 120.4a].

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text:
Yes. Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack; because it’s a triggered ability on the stack it is not a spell and therefore can’t be countered by effects that counter only spells, but it can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. 

Definition of key terms and supporting rules: 
- “Storm” is a triggered ability that functions on the stack: “Storm means ‘When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn…’” [702.40a].
- A triggered ability is an ability with a trigger condition and an effect that, once triggered, is put on the stack as an object that is not a card the next time a player would receive priority [603.1a; 603.3; 603.3d].
- Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells, so they can’t be countered by effects that counter only spells; they can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities [113.9].

Putting that together: storm creates a triggered ability that goes on the stack when its trigger occurs [702.40a; 603.3d]. That triggered ability is not a spell, so normal “counter target spell” effects can’t counter the storm ability, but any effect that specifically says it can counter abilities can counter the storm ability [113.9].

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text:
No. A card with a two-color hybrid mana symbol (for example {G/W}) is considered to have both colors in its color identity, so it can’t be put into a commander deck whose commander’s color identity lacks one of those colors. By contrast, a monocolored hybrid symbol (for example {2/B} or {C/G}) is still a colored symbol for that one color, so a card whose only colored mana symbols are of that single color can be included in a deck whose commander has that single color.

Definitions and reasoning
- Color identity: the color identity of a card is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text (plus any colors defined by characteristic-defining abilities or a color indicator). A card’s mana symbols determine which colors are in its color identity. [903.4]
- Hybrid mana symbol: a hybrid mana symbol is a mana symbol that can be paid in one of two ways and is also a colored mana symbol; it is all of its component colors. Monocolored hybrid symbols (such as {2/B} or {C/G}) are listed among hybrid symbols and count as the listed color even though one component is colorless or a number. [107.4e]
- How those rules interact: an object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost. If a mana symbol is hybrid and has two different colored components (for example {G/W}), the object is all of those component colors for color identity purposes; if the hybrid symbol’s nonnumeric component is a single color (for example {2/B}), that symbol contributes that one color to the object’s color identity. [202.2d] [107.4e] [903.4]

If you want a concrete check in a deck: look at every mana symbol in the card’s mana cost and rules text. If any of those symbols introduces a color the commander doesn’t have in its color identity, that card can’t be included in that commander deck. [903.4]

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text:
No. You can’t respond during the untap step: no player receives priority during the untap step, so players can’t cast spells or activate abilities then. (Untap step is the specific step in question.)

Definition of key terms: “Respond” for this question means taking actions that require priority (for example, casting spells, activating abilities, or taking other special actions). Priority is the game rule that determines who may take those actions; the player with priority may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions [117.1].

Why: The untap step gives no player priority, so the actions that require priority can’t be taken then [502.4]; this is reiterated by the rule that says no player receives priority during the untap step [117.3a]. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held until the next time a player would receive priority (usually the beginning of the upkeep), when those triggered abilities are put onto the stack and players may then act [502.4, 503.1a].

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes. A creature remains an attacking creature during the end of combat step; it stops being an attacking creature when it’s removed from combat or when the combat phase ends (which happens as soon as the end of combat step ends). Reasoning: “Attacking Creature” is defined as a creature that was declared as an attacker or was put onto the battlefield attacking, and it “remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first” [Attacking Creature]. The end of combat step is part of the combat phase [End of Combat Step], and “as soon as the end of combat step ends, all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat” (so they cease to be attacking at that point) [511.3]. Abilities that trigger “at end of combat” trigger as the end of combat step begins, while effects that last “until end of combat” expire at the end of the combat phase, consistent with creatures still being attacking during the step [511.2]. If a specific effect or event removed a creature from combat earlier (for example, one of the removal conditions in rule 506.4), that creature is no longer an attacking creature during the end of combat step [506.4].

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text:
No — you don’t cast lands. You play land cards as a special action (you “play a land”), you don’t cast them as spells. 

Definition and ruling: To play a land means to put that land onto the battlefield as a special action (a player may play a land only when they have priority during a main phase of their turn and the stack is empty). Playing a land doesn’t use the stack, the land isn’t a spell, and players can’t respond to the act of playing a land. Land cards normally have no mana cost and are played without paying any costs. If an object is both a land and another card type, that object can be played only as a land and can’t be cast as a spell. You also can’t play a land on an opponent’s turn. (See rules below.)

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text:
Yes. You can sacrifice a creature that was cast for its evoke cost after the creature’s evoke triggered ability has been put on the stack (i.e., in response to that triggered ability) so that when the evoke triggered ability later resolves it will no longer be able to cause that creature to be sacrificed.

Reasoning and definitions
- Evoke is defined as both an alternative-cost static ability and a triggered ability: “Evoke [cost]” means “You may cast this card by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost” and “When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it.” That triggered ability functions on the battlefield [702.74a].
- When the creature enters the battlefield the evoke triggered ability triggers. Once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3d]. That means you do not get priority to take actions before the evoke triggered ability is created and placed on the stack, but you do get priority with that triggered ability on the stack.
- While the triggered ability is on the stack, players may take actions (including sacrificing permanents). Abilities on the stack exist independently of their source, so the triggered ability will remain on the stack even if the creature is sacrificed in response [113.7a].
- If the creature is sacrificed in response, then when the evoke triggered ability resolves it will attempt to make its controller sacrifice the permanent, but if that controller no longer controls the creature (or controls no creatures eligible to be sacrificed for that instruction), the sacrifice can’t be performed (a player who controls no creatures can’t choose to sacrifice one) [608.2d].

Assumption about timing
- I assume you mean “before the evoke triggered ability resolves” in the usual sequence: creature enters → evoke ability triggers and is put on the stack → players receive priority and may act → the ability resolves. If you instead meant “before the evoke ability is even created and put on the stack,” that is not possible because the triggered ability is created and put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority after the creature enters [603.3d].

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text:
Yes. “Loses all abilities” includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are abilities (they’re presented as a keyword), and effects that remove abilities remove those abilities.

Definitions and brief reasoning:
- “Keyword ability”: an ability listed only by name on a card (a “keyword”) rather than a full sentence; keyword abilities are still abilities. [702.1]
- “Loses all abilities”: an effect that removes abilities from an object (it makes the object lose those abilities). Effects can add or remove abilities, and an effect that removes an ability removes all instances of that ability. [113.10] [113.10b] [113.10c]
- Because keyword abilities are abilities, an effect that causes an object to lose abilities removes its keyword abilities as well. [702.1] [113.10]
- Effects that say an object “can’t have” an ability cause it to lose that ability and prevent that ability from being added while that restriction applies. That applies to keyword abilities too. [113.11]
- For layering purposes, ability-adding effects, keyword counters, and ability-removing effects are applied together in the same layer, so interactions among those effects are resolved according to the continuous-effects rules. [613.1f]
- Note: an effect that instead sets a characteristic or states a quality of an object (for example, “is red” or “can’t be blocked”) is not the same as granting an ability; such effects aren’t “abilities” to be removed by a “lose abilities” effect. [113.12]

Assumption about wording: I’m treating “loses all abilities” as an effect that removes abilities from an object. If you meant some other wording, please quote it and I’ll apply these rules to that exact phrasing.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes. You may draw cards even if you already have as many cards as your maximum hand size; a player may have any number of cards in hand, and the maximum hand size only forces discarding during that player’s cleanup step. Definition: “maximum hand size” is the number of cards a player is allowed as their maximum (normally seven, modified by effects such as a vanguard card’s hand modifier). Definition: “draw a card” is the act of putting the top card of your library into your hand; when instructed to draw multiple cards, you perform that many individual draws. Rationale and rules: • A player may have any number of cards in their hand; the requirement to reduce to the maximum hand size happens as part of the cleanup step (they discard excess cards then) [402.2]. • The discard to maximum hand size during the cleanup step is a turn-based action that happens immediately at the beginning of the cleanup step and doesn’t use the stack [514.1] and [703.4n]. • A vanguard card’s hand modifier changes a player’s starting and maximum hand size (normally seven) [313.6] and [902.5b]. • If you are instructed to draw multiple cards, you do so one at a time [121.2b]. Practical effect: effects that cause you to draw while at or above your maximum hand size succeed and put those cards into your hand; you will only be required to discard down to your maximum during your cleanup step. (If you have a special case not covered here, tell me the exact effect and timing and I’ll apply the rules.)

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text:
If a planeswalker has exactly 0 loyalty counters, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action; the provided rules do not say what happens if a planeswalker has fewer than 0 loyalty counters.

Definitions and reasoning: "Loyalty counters" are counters on a planeswalker that indicate how much loyalty it has (the number of loyalty counters on a planeswalker equals its loyalty) [122.1e], [306.5c]. State-based actions are automatic game actions that happen whenever certain conditions are met and don’t use the stack [704.1]. The rules explicitly state that if a planeswalker has loyalty 0, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action [306.9], [704.5i]. (Damage can remove loyalty counters, because damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from it, which is one way a planeswalker can reach 0 loyalty) [306.8], [120.3c].

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No. Non-creature artifacts don’t “die.” The term dies applies only to creatures and planeswalkers; a permanent “dies” only if a creature or planeswalker is put into a graveyard from the battlefield [Dies], [700.4]. A non-creature artifact put into a graveyard from the battlefield is simply put into its owner’s graveyard (it doesn’t meet the definition of “dies”), though it can still be “destroyed” if an effect used the word “destroy” (destroy is a distinct concept; see [701.8b]) and objects put into graveyards go to their owners’ graveyards [404.1].

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text:
You lose the game the next time a player would receive priority if you attempt to draw a card from your library when it has no cards. (This is the direct result of attempting to draw from an empty library.)

Definitions and key points
- Draw: To draw a card means to put the top card of a player’s library into that player’s hand (see “Draw” and [121.1]). A player’s normal turn-based draw is the turn-based action that happens first in the draw step ([504.1]).
- State-based actions and timing: State-based actions are checked automatically and don’t use the stack ([704.1]). If you attempted to draw from an empty library, you lose the game the next time a player would receive priority ([121.4]; see the repetition of this in the list of state-based actions, [704.5b]).

Related interactions you should know about
- Replacement effects that replace draws are applied even if no cards could be drawn because the library is empty ([121.6a]; [614.11]). Whether a draw is replaced can change what actually happens, because replacement effects are applied in place of the draw. 
- If an effect offers a choice to draw a card when the affected player’s library is empty, that choice can be taken (unless another effect says that player can’t draw cards) ([121.3]; [121.3a]).
- If an effect moves cards from a library to a hand without using the word “draw,” those cards are not considered drawn; that matters for draw triggers and replacement effects, and for the empty-library loss consequences ([121.5]).
- If an effect tries to move cards out of a library (as opposed to drawing) and fewer cards exist than requested, it moves as many as possible ([609.3]); similarly, if you’re required to draw more cards than remain, you draw the remaining cards and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority ([104.3c]).

Example (common case): During your draw step you would draw but your library is empty. You’ve attempted to draw from an empty library, so you will lose the game the next time a player would receive priority ([504.1]; [121.4]; [704.5b]). If a replacement effect replaces that draw, apply the replacement effect (replacement effects are applied even if no cards could be drawn, [121.6a]; [614.11]), and the result depends on the replacement’s effect (for instance, if the replacement moves cards without using the word “draw,” those cards aren’t draws, [121.5]).

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
Direct answer: The combat phase has five steps in this order—beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat—and the defending player is the nonactive player in a two-player game or is determined as described for multiplayer before beginning of combat. You (as the defending player) get priority only when the active player has priority and then passes priority to you; the active player receives priority at the beginning of most steps (after any turn‑based actions and trigger placement), and some combat steps contain turn‑based actions that happen before priority is given.

Details and how this works in practice
- Combat steps: The combat phase consists of beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat (in that order). If no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking, the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped (so the phase can be shorter) [506.1] [508.8].
- Who is the defending player: In a two‑player game, the defending player is the nonactive player for the combat phase [506.2] [506.2a]. In multiplayer, if the variant makes all opponents defending players, then all opponents are defending players for the combat phase [802.2]; otherwise the active player chooses one opponent as the defending player as a turn‑based action immediately after the beginning of combat step begins (this choice doesn’t use the stack) [507.1] [703.4h] [506.2a].
- What “priority” means: Priority is the right to take actions (cast spells, activate abilities, take special actions). Which player has priority is determined by the priority rules: the player with priority may act [117.1].
- When the defending player gets priority during combat: The active player receives priority at the beginning of most steps and phases after any turn‑based actions are done and any triggered abilities for that step are put on the stack. That means when a combat step begins and any required turn‑based actions for that step are completed (for example, choosing a defending player at the beginning of combat), the active player will have priority first; the defending player will only get priority if and when the active player passes priority to them [117.3a] [507.1] [703.4h]. For example, once the end of combat step begins, the active player gets priority immediately (the defending player does not get priority first) [511.1].
- Combat damage step specifics: As a turn‑based action at the beginning of the combat damage step, players announce how their creatures assign combat damage: first the active player announces how attacking creatures assign, then the defending player announces how blocking creatures assign (this announcement doesn’t use the stack and follows APNAP order in multiplayer). After assignments are announced, all assigned combat damage is dealt simultaneously; there is no opportunity to cast spells or activate abilities between assignment and dealing [703.4k] [510.1] [802.5] [510.2].

Timing note (assumption): The above assumes the normal order of steps and that you mean “when do I get priority during the combat phase.” If you meant a specific instant (for example, immediately after an attacker is declared or immediately after damage is assigned), the same rule applies: the active player gets priority at the start of the step after turn‑based actions are done, and you (the defending player) get priority only after the active player passes [117.3a] [703.4k] [510.2].

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text:
No. You can’t respond to a mana ability: a mana ability doesn’t use the stack and resolves immediately when it’s activated, so it can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to (605.3b; 405.6c). 

Definition — “mana ability”: an activated or triggered ability that could add mana to a player’s mana pool and doesn’t use the stack (605.1a; Mana Ability). “Respond” in this context means putting spells or abilities onto the stack (see 602.2), which you can’t do to affect a mana ability because it does not use the stack (605.3b). 

Triggered mana abilities: a triggered mana ability likewise doesn’t go on the stack and is added/resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority, so you can’t respond to that either (605.4a). 

Important exception: an ability that has a target is not a mana ability and thus uses the stack and can be responded to; only abilities that meet the mana-ability criteria are unrespondable (605.5a). Also note when you may activate mana abilities: players may activate mana abilities whenever they have priority or while casting/activating something that asks for mana (117.1d).
